query_text: Should corporations be required to pay taxes on all profits?

messages.content: Should corporations be required to pay taxes on all profits?

message.content:
Whether corporations **should** be required to pay taxes on *all* profits is a **policy question**, not a settled fact. In the U.S. today, corporations are generally taxed on their net income, but many profitable corporations can end up owing little or no federal income tax because of deductions, credits, accelerated depreciation, losses, and other provisions.[1][2][3][5]

A few key points shape the debate:

- **Current system:** C corporations are separate taxpaying entities, and profits can be taxed at the corporate level and again when paid out as dividends, creating “double taxation.”[2][4]
- **Not all businesses are taxed this way:** S corporations and many LLCs are pass-through entities, so business profits are taxed on owners’ personal returns instead of at the entity level.[4][7]
- **Why some favor taxing all profits:** Supporters argue it would reduce avoidance and ensure profitable corporations pay at least some tax in profitable years; advocacy groups have documented large corporations paying zero federal income tax despite significant pretax income.[3][5]
- **Why others oppose it:** Critics note that taxing *all* profits without deductions would ignore legitimate business expenses, investment costs, and losses, and could discourage capital investment or amplify double taxation.[1][2][4]

If you mean “Should corporations pay tax on **net profits after legitimate expenses**?”, that is the standard corporate-income-tax model used in the U.S.[1][2][7] If you mean “Should corporations pay tax on **every dollar of accounting profit with no deductions at all**?”, that is a much more aggressive proposal and would represent a major departure from current tax design.[1][4][5]
